title: Micro-scheduler and Slab-Cache CUDA Shim: exploratory probe
content:
Summary:

This note captures an early, focused experiment: implement a thin CUDA "shim" layer that sits between the serving runtime scheduler and downstream model execution backends (TensorRT runtime, Triton/TFRT paths, and our custom fused CUDA kernels). The shim exposes two runtime primitives the scheduler can rely on: 1) micro-schedule slots (time-sliced GPU worker tokens) and 2) a slab-based KV-cache allocator with eviction hints. The goal is to evaluate tradeoffs for latency tail, throughput under mixed-load, and integration complexity compared to our heavier interop approaches.

Why we tried this (motivation):
- Observed pain: when mix of short-chat and long-completion requests hit GPUs, full model-level batching and kernel-switching causes long scheduling delays and KV cache thrash. Existing approaches (heavy-weight kernel adapters or full Triton integration) add complexity and still produce tail spikes during phase changes.
- Hypothesis: A small, predictable shim exposing two primitives (micro-schedule + slab cache) can reduce scheduling jitter, make eviction decisions lightweight, and allow cheaper fallback to lower-precision kernels without major refactor.

Design overview (high level):
- Shim responsibilities (minimal):
  - Provide micro-scheduler tokens: small-duration GPU time-slices (e.g., 2–8 ms) that a session can hold to run incremental decode iterations. Tokens can be yielded to allow fair interleaving of many short-running decodes.
  - Provide slab-based KV cache allocator: pre-allocated memory slabs sized to common prefix lengths (e.g., 8KB, 32KB, 128KB). Each active session maps to one or more slabs. Shim records last-access timestamps and a lightweight ‘reuse score’ (exponentially weighted hit-rate) for eviction ranking.
  - Abstract backend submission: commands are forwarded to the chosen backend (TRT engine, Triton, or custom kernel) but all memory setup and token acquisition go through the shim.

API contract (shim <-> scheduler):
- request_token(session_id, preferred_duration_ms) -> token_id or queued
- release_token(token_id) -> void
- alloc_slab(session_id, slab_size_hint) -> slab_handle or OOM
- touch_slab(slab_handle, offset, length) -> mark hot
- slab_eviction_candidates(max_count) -> list of slab_handles (non-blocking)
- submit_exec(token_id, backend, exec_descriptor) -> future(exec_result)

Micro-scheduling semantics:
- Tokens are cheap and preallocated per GPU worker thread pool. When demand spikes, token queue uses approximate fair queuing: sessions are ordered by last-served time and reuse-score to avoid starving long-running decode that steadily advances.
- If an execution cannot finish within preferred_duration_ms, the backend is expected to yield at safe preemption points (we add yield hooks at decoder-loop boundaries). Backend fallback (e.g., switch to a lighter kernel) is allowed when token expires more than twice in a row.

Slab-cache semantics and eviction policy:
- We group KV memory into power-of-two slab sizes. Slabs are bound to sessions but can be reassigned when eviction occurs.
- Eviction rank = alpha * recency_score + beta * reuse_score - gamma * pinned_score. We tune alpha/beta/gamma in experiments.
- Eviction is cooperative: shim returns candidate list, scheduler decides whether to re-route to a lower-cost model variant or to spill to host memory.

Integration points and backends:
- TensorRT path: shim sets up device pointers and provides a pinned slab handle; TRT engines are executed unchanged except for decode loop yields where we return control to the shim. We tested two patterns: (a) embedding the yield inside a custom TRT plugin, (b) running TRT in short-run loops and re-enqueuing.
- Triton path: shim acts as a custom backend that manages slab lifetimes and token checks; Triton worker threads call into shim pre/post model invocation.
- Custom fused kernels: we built a minimal decoder kernel that accepts a slab_handle and respects yield points. These kernels can do in-place KV updates to avoid copies.

Experiment setup (what we ran):
- Hardware: 4x A100 40GB per node; workload driver runs synthetic mixes.
- Models: GPT-like open model, 2B quant-aware variant, and a small 300M BPE chat model.
- Workloads: three mixes — short-chat heavy (80% short 16-token responses), mixed (50/50 short/long), and long completions heavy (80% 256-token tails).
- Baselines: current kernel-switcher (no shim) and Triton+full-adapter integration.
- Metrics: p50/p90/p99 latency per step, end-to-end request latency, GPU utilization, slab eviction rate, number of spills to host, throughput (tokens/s).

Key observations (empirical):
- Tail reduction: micro-scheduling with 4ms default tokens reduced p99 step latency by ~28% on mixed workloads compared to baseline. Improvement came primarily from reduced queueing while long decode sessions made progress in interleaved small increments.
- Eviction stability: slab allocator with three slab sizes reduced reallocation churn vs naive per-session malloc. Spills to host dropped 40% for mixed workloads when tuned reuse_score priority high.
- Backend overhead: embedding the yield inside a TRT plugin added ~0.6ms overhead per yield vs short-run reenqueue approach which added ~1.2ms due to API overheads. So plugin approach is preferable where we can extend TRT.
- Fallback switching: automatic fallback to lighter quant kernels after two consecutive token expirations lowered tail but reduced output quality in a measurable way for certain prompts (we saw small perplexity regressions). This underscores need to tie fallback decisions to eval metrics, not only scheduling pressure.
- Contention scenario: under extreme concurrency (>200 active sessions per GPU), micro-scheduler added extra CPU scheduling load and we observed diminished returns. There is a practical concurrency knee where hybrid per-GPU worker pool size must be tuned.

Tradeoffs (summary):
- Complexity vs benefits: shim is relatively low-friction to introduce for our runtime because it isolates memory and token semantics. It requires some backend cooperation (yield hooks or short-run loops) to perform best.
- Latency fairness: micro-scheduling improves fairness for short requests but can increase median latency for large single-session runs unless token durations are adaptive.
- Memory behavior: slab caching reduces allocation churn and fragmentation but can increase fragmentation if slab sizes are poorly matched to ephemeral prefix distributions.
- Quality impact: any automatic kernel fallback must be gated by quality checks (per-route evals) — otherwise we trade latency for model quality in ways product teams will notice.

Open questions / next experiments:
- Adaptive token sizing: evaluate auto-scaling token_duration based on observed per-session step time distribution (exponential moving average) rather than fixed ms.
- Hybrid reclaim: allow eligible slabs to be temporarily compressed (FP16->INT8 in-place via quantize helpers) as an intermediate reclaim action before eviction. Measure cost/benefit.
- Scheduler backpressure signals: add explicit backpressure to gateways to avoid overload; measure upstream QoS improvement when gateway refuses or redirects requests rather than letting them pile into micro-scheduler queue.
- Long tail pathological cases: construct adversarial mixes that repeatedly force yields at identical offsets; measure whether any fairness starvation emerges and how to protect against it.

Implementation notes & TODOs:
- Proof-of-concept shim implemented in runtime/shim/ with ~1.2k LOC C++ + CUDA (prototype branch linked). Needs cleanup and unit tests.
- Add metrics: slab_age, slab_reuse, token_wait_time, yields_per_request. Hook into console dashboards under per-route panels.
- Policy UI: add console knobs for alpha/beta/gamma weights and token default duration.
- RFC to coordinate with model-ops: define per-model quality signal for safe fallback (thresholds + eval set).

Conclusion:
The micro-scheduler + slab-cache shim is promising: it gives predictable, low-level primitives that reduce queueing tail and memory churn while keeping backend integration surface small. It is not a silver bullet — we need adaptive token sizing and careful quality gating for kernel fallback. Next steps are to harden the prototype, run longer soak tests with real traffic traces, and build a small control plane UI for policy tuning.

Appendix: quick notes from the run
- Best config observed: token=4ms, slab sizes [8KB, 32KB, 128KB], eviction weights alpha=1.0, beta=2.5, gamma=3.0.
- Measured p99 step latencies (mixed workload): baseline 92ms -> shim 66ms -> shim+w/ plugin TRT yield 62ms.
- Key PRs: runtime/shim prototype (PR 482), custom TRT plugin sketch (PR 498).

Contact & next sync:
Ping @Ravi and @Lena for a Monday sync to select experiments for a 2-week run; I'll open an RFC for token autosizing by next Friday.

(Notes: this doc is exploratory and includes rough numbers from limited runs — treat as prototyping output, not production guarantees.)
